transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-28
Start: 10:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jamal Reed (Redwood CSM), Mark Delgado (Waypoint Head of ML), Sara Kim (Waypoint Platform Eng), Tom Rivera (Waypoint CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may be fuzzy): review of KV cache hit improvements after tuning, discussion of prefix caching strategy for checkout flows, decisions on next benchmark runs and security doc requests.

[00:00] Alex Monroe: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly caching sync. I think we have a full house - quick roll call?
[00:07] Mark Delgado: Mark here.
[00:09] Sara Kim: Sara - hi.
[00:11] Tom Rivera: Tom, good morning.
[00:12] Priya Kapoor: Priya from Redwood, hey all.
[00:14] Jamal Reed: Jamal on the call.
[00:16] Alex Monroe: Great. Agenda - quick results review, dig into KV prefix hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, and agree next steps.

[02:05] Priya Kapoor: Ok, so we ran the replay you sent over last week, Mark, thanks for that. I pulled together two runs: baseline (no caching changes) and tuned (prefix length + TTL adjustments, and KV cache warms). The headline: KV cache global hit rate moved from about 42% baseline to roughly 68% on tuned config, but that's across all flows. For the checkout microflow specifically, hit rate is higher, about 75%.
[02:35] Mark Delgado: Wait, 68% overall? That's big, that would materially lower token cost. How are you measuring hits - per-key or per-token?
[02:42] Priya Kapoor: It's per-key cache hit on the KV store. We also computed token-savings estimate by multiplying average continuation length; that gave an estimated token reduction of ~28% for the tuned run. There is some noise in the logs so take that as an estimate.
[03:10] Sara Kim: Noise how? Like alignment mismatch between prompts?
[03:13] Priya Kapoor: Exactly, transcription/parsing differences and some prompt variants where user metadata changes the prefix slightly. We normalized by stripping session IDs and user names, that helped a lot. But there are still a few templating differences - e.g., currency symbol variations - that break prefix equality.
[03:40] Tom Rivera: Could we canonicalize those before hitting the model? That seems low-hanging.
[03:45] Mark Delgado: Yeah, we already have a canonicalizer for addresses; adding currency/locale normalization is doable. But curious - what's the prefix cache vs KV cache distinction here?
[03:55] Priya Kapoor: Good question. Prefix cache is server-side caching of input prefixes -> cached model state (KV cache snapshot essentially), so when two requests share a long common prompt prefix, we can reuse the KV cache and only generate remaining tokens. KV cache in our metrics refers to both the prefix snapshot reuse and token-level internal kv hits. In the replay we separated them but some customers conflate terms - sorry if that's confusing.
[04:25] Alex Monroe: No worries - for decision making we usually look at 'effective reuse' which bundles both.

[05:10] Priya Kapoor: One caveat: larger prefix reuse increases memory pressure on runtime nodes and can slightly increase p50 latency when we restore large KV snapshots, so there's a tradeoff. In tuned run we set a snapshot size limit of 2MB and TTL of 12 minutes; that gave the 68% hit rate with p95 latency still within your SLO of 500ms for the checkout flow. p99 did rise by ~80ms in spikes.
[05:44] Sara Kim: p99 rising is our big concern - our storefront SLA has 300ms target for interactive chat. Are those numbers for hosted or dedicated?
[05:51] Priya Kapoor: These runs were on a hosted-like config but using reserved capacity nodes (so roughly dedicated performance). If you move to Dedicated with pinned instances and optimized kernel selection, the p99 will tighten. We can run an explicit p99 bench on dedicated nodes next week.

[07:20] Mark Delgado: Can you remind me of the prompt reuse strategy you suggested last week? I want to make sure we implement correctly.
[07:25] Priya Kapoor: Sure - two parts: 1) canonicalize user-specific tokens (IDs, timestamps, currencies) to increase shared prefix matches, and 2) restructure prompts to push stable context earlier in the prefix so more of it becomes reusable. For instance, put system instructions and product catalog excerpts up front, then session/user specifics later.
[07:48] Tom Rivera: That makes sense. Do we lose signal if we canonicalize too aggressively? For personalization we still need some user tokens.
[07:55] Priya Kapoor: Right - it's about selective canonicalization. Keep personalization tokens but move them or hash them into a smaller canonical slot that doesn't break earlier prefix. Also consider using retrieval + embeddings for user-specific data rather than raw tokens in the prompt.
[08:20] Alex Monroe: Quick note: retrieval plus embedding lookups can increase latency if not cached appropriately - so you'd want that to be cached in your app layer or use Redwood's response caching for embeddings.

[09:40] Mark Delgado: What about batching - you mentioned a +30% larger batch window for KV replay. What's the effect on latency?
[09:47] Priya Kapoor: Increasing batch window during replay is only for offline replay analysis to increase effective aggregation and hit rates. For production, adaptive batching in Redwood can be tuned to keep p50/p95 low. There's a tradeoff: larger batching increases throughput and token economy but hurts tail latency. For your checkout flow we recommend conservative batching (max 8 requests or 20ms window) to keep p95 under target.
[10:15] Sara Kim: OK. From infra side, we need to see the config you used - TTLs, snapshot limit, eviction policy - to map into our deployment.
[10:22] Priya Kapoor: Yes we'll share the config JSON after the call.

[12:00] Jamal Reed: Quick pause for security/compliance items - Tom, Mark, you had asked for SOC 2 docs and KMS integration notes. We actually uploaded those to the shared drive, link in the notes. Tom, you had a question about audit logs and retention?
[12:13] Tom Rivera: Yeah, retention. Do you keep prompt-level logs by default? We need to limit retention for PII and have a way to redact.
[12:20] Jamal Reed: By default hosted keeps 30 days; for Private or Dedicated we can configure retention and you can use customer-managed KMS for encryption. We also offer a redaction hook in the ingestion pipeline to scrub PII before it hits storage. I'll follow up with the exact artifact.
[12:40] Tom Rivera: OK please share SOC2 and the API for redaction.

[13:10] Priya Kapoor: Back to hit rates - we also tested a prefix-only strategy (no KV snapshots, only text prefix matching) and that gave a smaller win - about 22% effective token reduction - because your prompts have long stable system instructions that benefit from snapshotting. So KV snapshots plus canonicalization is giving the best ROI.
[13:40] Mark Delgado: What were the cold-start effects? New sessions obviously won't get hits.
[13:45] Priya Kapoor: Cold start was visible: roughly first 10 requests per user session had near-zero reuse, then reuse ramped. For typical checkout flows (3-6 interactions) you get limited reuse unless you pre-warm using our client-side prefetch pattern. We recommended prefetching the system prompt snapshot when the user lands on checkout page. That increases initial hit rate.
[14:30] Sara Kim: Does prefetching increase token costs?
[14:33] Priya Kapoor: It does - you pay for the prefetch call but overall it often reduces net tokens because subsequent responses are much shorter. We can model that with a quick cost simulation.

[16:05] Mark Delgado: Can we see a per-flow breakdown? You mentioned checkout was 75% hit, what about returns, support chat?
[16:12] Priya Kapoor: Yes in the report: checkout ~75%, returns ~58%, post-purchase support ~44%. Support has a lot of variable user text so canonicalization helps less.

[17:25] Alex Monroe: Let's talk numbers that matter for procurement - if we get 28% token reduction overall, what's the projected monthly savings on your current load?
[17:33] Priya Kapoor: Using your reported 250M tokens/month baseline, a 28% reduction is roughly 70M tokens saved. At your committed dedicated pricing tier that translates to approximately $12-16k/month saving, after factoring in caching storage cost and a small increase in node memory. We'll send a detailed cost appendix.

[19:00] Sara Kim: On the Dedicated vs Hosted question - will moving to Dedicated reduce the p99 spikes you saw?
[19:07] Priya Kapoor: Yes, Dedicated with pinned GPUs and tuned kernel selection reduces variance. Also we can enable faster serialization paths for KV restore. But it does add cost; we'll outline tradeoffs in the pricing note.

[21:10] Mark Delgado: Any concerns about cache poisoning or stale state with long TTLs?
[21:15] Priya Kapoor: Good point. We recommend conservative TTLs for flows with time-sensitive info and an eviction policy based on usage recency. For sensitive data, enable explicit invalidation on user events (e.g., order status change) - we support an invalidation API. Also monitor divergence and set alerts if the downstream QA score drops.

[23:00] Tom Rivera: What about model rollouts? If we change model weights, can cached snapshots become incompatible?
[23:08] Priya Kapoor: Yes, KV snapshots are model-version specific. Redwood tags snapshot metadata with model and tokenizer version; during a model switch we either invalidate or maintain parallel caches for the old/new model during a canary rollout. We'll show the rollout pattern in the docs.

[26:40] Priya Kapoor: Ok, technical ask - Mark, can you provide two additional representative prompt sets: (1) multi-step checkout with discounts and coupons, (2) returns flow with attachments. Those will help exercise canonicalization rules.
[26:55] Mark Delgado: Yep we'll share those by Friday.

[28:12] Alex Monroe: On the benchmark side, Priya will run an expanded KV replay with a +30% batch window to see whether hit rates improve further; then we'll run a p99 latency bench constrained to your SLOs. Priya, timeline?
[28:23] Priya Kapoor: I can run the replay by next Tuesday and share raw CSV + analysis by Wednesday. The p99 bench I'll coordinate for Friday when we have the new prompt sets.

[30:05] Sara Kim: Also we need the security artifacts: SOC2, redaction API, KMS integration doc, and audit log retention options. Jamal?
[30:12] Jamal Reed: I'll drop links in the notes and follow up with a short doc summarizing retention controls and the redaction webhook - by EOD today.

[32:40] Mark Delgado: A couple of smaller items - can we get the exact caching config you used (TTL, snapshot limit, eviction policy) as JSON and an example of the prefetch call?
[32:50] Priya Kapoor: Yes, I'll copy that into a config file and share. It'll include the TTL=720s, snapshot_limit=2MB, eviction=LRU with explicit invalidation. That's what produced the tuned results.

[34:00] Tom Rivera: One operational question: when we do shared prefix snapshots, how do you handle multi-tenant isolation? We need to make sure our customers' data is never mixed.
[34:09] Priya Kapoor: All snapshots are scoped to tenant (account_id). We never create cross-tenant shares. If you use a shared tenant model, there are additional flags but we won't enable those.

[35:30] Alex Monroe: Anything else on the technical side?
[35:35] Sara Kim: Not from me. We'll validate the config and give feedback.

[37:00] Priya Kapoor: Quick note about prompt hashing - we use configurable normalization hooks; if you want, we can give you the normalizer library to run inside your preprocessing pipeline to maximize hit rates before traffic reaches Redwood.
[37:15] Mark Delgado: Send it over.

[38:30] Alex Monroe: Ok, recap and next steps: Redwood to run KV replay (+30% batch window) and share results; Priya to share config JSON and normalizer lib; Jamal to send SOC2/KMS/redaction docs; Waypoint to provide prompt sets and validate firewall/VPC items. We'll target the p99 bench next week.

[39:20] Tom Rivera: Sounds good. One note: please include conservative numbers in your pricing projection - procurement will want worst-case and best-case.

[40:00] Priya Kapoor: I'll also include a short appendix on how to invalidate caches on order updates and an example API call.

[41:10] Mark Delgado: Great. Thanks everyone.
